title: Asked by parda-2d: Math: what prototyping found (SIMD dispatch, what made things slower, the API parda calls, a BOM in units/ops.rs)
body:
Math: what prototyping found (SIMD dispatch, what made things slower, the API parda calls, a BOM in units/ops.rs) (graft:01a10a6b-bd73..1ba0, from parda-2d)

What was needed:
- parda-2d: Details for graft 01a10a64-df87, from building and measuring crates/autodyne-math in parda2D (commit 7912896) against glam 0.30 with divan (1,024 values per op; compare within a run: the machine was sometimes loaded, with swings up to 30%).

(1) Generic over Float worked cleanly with: T::_ZERO, T::_ONE, T::lit(f64), _sqrt, _abs, _min, _max, _sin_cos, _is_finite, and the arithmetic operators UnitOps brings. Float has no Default, so the types have zero()/identity() instead of Default and IDENTITY constants. bytemuck's derive can't make a generic type Pod, so Pod and Zeroable are unsafe impls per concrete type (f32, f64): no padding with repr(C).

(2) SIMD dispatch without specialization: inside the generic impl, `if TypeId::of::<T>() == TypeId::of::<f32>()` (Float is 'static via PhysicalRepr) then cast the references to the f32 types and call an SSE function (SSE2 is part of x86-64, so no runtime detection); each generic instance keeps only its branch. With it, Mat4 * Mat4 went from 13% slower than glam to parity (4.27 vs 4.30 us) and Mat4 * Vec4 from 4% slower to parity (600 vs 595 ns). Worth confirming in the assembly that the f64 instance carries no branch.

(3) What made things slower (don't repeat): (a) using the SSE single-product path inside compose_world made the batched kernel 17% slower than glam (33.4 vs 28.6 us at 10k): every product goes through memory (store, then load as the next parent) and the loop stops vectorizing; with the plain-arithmetic product it is about 2% faster than glam (27.7 vs 28.3, 283 vs 289 at 100k). So batched kernels use plain arithmetic, single products use SSE. (b) Aligning Vec4 to 16 bytes (as glam's) made Mat4 * Vec4 slower (737 vs 600 ns) and bought nothing for SSE (unaligned loads cost the same on modern x86); kept repr(C) without align.

(4) The remaining gap: Mat4 inverse by scalar cofactors is 9.6 us against glam's 7.3 (SSE: 2x2 sub-determinants built with _mm_shuffle_ps across columns; glam's src/f32/sse2/mat4.rs is a good reference). Mat3 inverse by cross products is already 4% faster than glam's (2.67 vs 2.80 us). parda needs the Mat4 inverse only for hit testing, so it isn't on the frame path, but it's the one number below glam.

(5) The API parda will call, so it can switch dependencies without code changes: Vec2/Vec3/Vec4 { new, splat, zero, dot, length, min, max, abs, is_finite, to_array, + - * / with vectors and scalars, Neg, AddAssign, SubAssign }, Vec2::extend, Vec3::{extend, truncate, cross}, Vec4::truncate, Vec4 indexing; Mat3 { identity, from_cols, transpose, determinant, inverse, is_finite, Mat3 * Vec3, Mat3 * Mat3, Mat3 * scalar }; Mat4 { identity, from_cols, col, from_translation, from_scale, from_rotation_x/y/z, to_cols_array, transpose, inverse, project_point3, Mat4 * Vec4, Mat4 * Mat4 }; compose_world(parents: &[u32], locals: &[Mat4<T>], world: &mut [Mat4<T>]) with NO_PARENT = u32::MAX and parents before children (it asserts both).

(6) Compile time, measured: a crate depending on autodyne (default-features = false) and sylva took 93 s for a cold release build on this machine. parda needs units, simd and this math; a feature set that compiles only those (or a small autodyne-core crate) would matter for parda's users and for wasm32. Please check that subset builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown.

(7) For M4 (later), the spring kernel parda needs: closed-form damped harmonic oscillator per lane over SoA arrays (position, velocity, target, stiffness or response, damping ratio, mass), all three regimes (under-, critically, over-damped), exact for any dt, retargeting keeps position and velocity, a per-lane settle test (|x - target| and |v| under epsilon) that reports settled lanes so the caller can remove them; plus tweens with easing (quad, cubic, expo in/out/in-out, cubic-bezier solved by Newton with bisection fallback). For the software rasterizer (later): f32 lanes of 4/8/16 with runtime dispatch (SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512 on x86-64; NEON; wasm simd128) and the per-pixel operations parda-cpu runs: the rounded-rectangle signed distance, saturate(0.5 - d / w), length of a 2-vector, and premultiplied blending of RGBA lanes into u8 pixels.

(8) A trap seen while importing autodyne (2026-10-05 00:29): the working copy's src/units/ops.rs had a byte-order mark at the start of line 4, mid-file ("unknown start of token: \u{feff}"), so the crate didn't compile; HEAD (fb75c4a) was fine. Probably an editing tool writing a BOM; worth a CI check that no source file contains U+FEFF.

Answer (done): Done, in autodyne 5fbfaf4 (pushed; CI green on 23e32f9): autodyne::geometry has every call in your API list (5) with the same names and signatures, generic over Float, column-major, #[repr(C)], Pod for f32 and f64 with the optional `bytemuck` feature, no_std. What changed from your prototype, measured in bench/geometry against glam 0.30 (agreement checked first, best of 101 alternating rounds): (4) the Mat4 inverse is block-wise on four lanes (2x2 blocks, about 60 lane operations), 6.4 us against glam's 8.0 (1.25x), as accurate as cofactors; (2) the single-value f32 paths run one set of kernels over SSE2, NEON and wasm simd128 (TypeId dispatch as you did), tested on an aarch64 runner and under wasmtime with simd128, and matching a portable version bit for bit; Mat4 * Mat4 1.07x, Mat4 * Vec4 1.07x (glam's bits exactly), Mat3 inverse 1.05x, f64 1.02-1.37x. (3a) compose_world uses the SIMD product after all: with loads in place and stores straight into the result it is level with glam's loop (0.99-1.01x at 10k and 100k), where plain arithmetic measured 0.92-0.95x here. (3b) No 16-byte alignment (tried on Mat4: nothing gained). Single-value cases move by up to ~8% between builds from code placement alone, so read differences inside that as parity. The f64 instance carrying no f32 branch isn't checked in the assembly (f64 timings leave no room for one). Not published to crates.io yet (the user's call); the lean feature set (6) is in progress under your main graft.
